scenario.name: Microsoft MSRC & CISA KEV DFIR — ASP.NET / SharePoint __VIEWSTATE MachineKey LosFormatter Deserialization Forensics
scenario.overview: A web office sends visitors a folded state receipt stamped with a secret office seal so the clerk trusts any receipt brought back later. Once an outsider steals the secret sealing key from the office supply book, they forge a spring-loaded receipt that unpacks straight into a live command terminal under the clerk badge. In this scenario (T1190, Microsoft MSRC & CISA KEV DFIR, ASP.NET / SharePoint __VIEWSTATE MachineKey LosFormatter Deserialization Forensics), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: web.config <machineKey> validationKey, then signed __VIEWSTATE LosFormatter /, then w3wp.exe Child Process Creation. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering web.config <machineKey> validationKey, then Signed __VIEWSTATE LosFormatter /, then w3wp.exe Child Process Creation, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection correlates Sysmon Event 1 with the documented host and network chain.

stages.title: Stage 2: Signed __VIEWSTATE LosFormatter / TypeConfuseDelegate Deserialization (IIS W3C Access Log)
stages.subtitle: Execution (T1059 - Signed LosFormatter .NET Gadget Deserialization)
stages.description: Once the seal checks out, the outsider submits a bulky, validly stamped receipt containing a chain of self-triggering parts. Trusting the valid wax seal, the office clerk unfolds the receipt and accidentally triggers arbitrary code. Once the attacker obtains the web.config validationKey (via a path traversal, backup leak, or CVE-2023-29357 auth bypass), they sign a TypeConfuseDelegate / ActivitySurrogateSelector gadget chain with HMACSHA256 and submit it via POST /_layouts/15/Picker.aspx (or GET ?__VIEWSTATE=/wEPDwUK...). Because the HMAC is valid, HTTP 200 is returned in the IIS W3C log (C:\inetpub\logs\LogFiles\W3SVC1\u_ex*.log) with an abnormally large cs-bytes (request size) or cs-uri-query (logged in Network Event 200 with LogFile=C:\inetpub\logs\LogFiles\W3SVC1\u_ex261103.log, UriStem=/_layouts/15/Picker.aspx, RequestBytes=cs-bytes=8420 , Signed ObjectStateFormatter Payload, HttpStatus=200 OK , HMAC Validation Passed so analysts can verify the exact actor and target artifact). Under the hood, the observed step executes IIS W3C Log Fields: date time c-ip cs-method cs-uri-stem cs-uri-query sc-status sc-bytes cs-bytes (which executes the technical command / telemetry directive , IIS W3C Log Fields: date time c-ip cs-method cs-uri-stem cs-uri-query sc-status sc-bytes cs so that advances the scenario kill-chain under MITRE T1059 during "Signed __VIEWSTATE LosFormatter / TypeConfuseDelegate Deserialization , IIS W3C Access Log" , Once the attacker obtains the web while generating verifiable host or network telemetry for DFIR attribution). Next, the follow-up artifact Anomaly: POST /_layouts/15/Picker.aspx sc-status=200 cs-bytes=8420 (Large signed __VIEWSTATE) runs (which executes the technical command / telemetry directive , Anomaly: POST /_layouts/15/Picker.aspx sc-status=200 cs-bytes=8420 , Large signed __VIEWSTAT so that advances the scenario kill-chain under MITRE T1059 during "Signed __VIEWSTATE LosFormatter / TypeConfuseDelegate Deserialization , IIS W3C Access Log" , Once the attacker obtains the web while generating verifiable host or network telemetry for DFIR attribution). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ IIS W3C: POST /_layouts/15/Picker.aspx sc-status=200 cs-bytes=8420 / ⇠#2 RESP 200) from Node ② (#2 DMZ Reverse Proxy & SPAN Tap) to Node ③ (#3 IIS W3C Extended Log (:443)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 web.config <machineKey>).
